introduction.p: Numbers do two jobs for us. They locate points, and they measure distances between points. The same number 3 can mean a position on a line, a length, a time, a temperature, or an error bound. Calculus depends on moving between these meanings without confusion.

subsection.title: Points as numbers
subsection.p: We picture the real numbers on a horizontal line. Positive numbers lie to the right of 0. Negative numbers lie to the left.

subsection.title: Open, closed, and half-open intervals
subsection.p: An interval is an unbroken piece of the real line. If two numbers are in the interval, then every number between them is also in the interval.

The parentheses mean that an endpoint is not included. The square bracket means that an endpoint is included.

description.p: Open circles mean endpoints are excluded. Filled circles mean endpoints are included.

The symbols \infty and -\infty are not real numbers. They are directions. So we never write a square bracket next to \infty.

paragraphs.title: Why \varepsilon>0 appears
paragraphs.p: The number \varepsilon is usually an allowed error. Allowed errors must be positive.

So whenever we write |x-a|<\varepsilon to describe closeness, we mean \varepsilon>0.

exercise.title: What does |x-a|<\varepsilon say in ordinary language?

statement.p: The inequality |x-a|<\varepsilon is equivalent to a-\varepsilon<x<a+\varepsilon. In your own words, why is absolute value a distance, and why must the allowed error \varepsilon be positive?

hint.p: Distance is never negative. An allowed error of 0 would demand that two numbers coincide, which is not a neighborhood of nearby values.

subsection.p: Rational numbers measure many distances, but they do not represent every point required by geometry and limiting processes. The next section explains why the real numbers are needed.
The answer is yes for the real numbers. It is no for the rational numbers. That difference is one reason calculus is built on \mathbb R, not just on fractions.
